This game is honestly one of my favorite games I have played in a while. Very time consuming especially after they stop helping as much as they did in the first chapters but worth it. This game is definitely something I would recommend if you like detective games with a bit of hacking and spying. 

The first 3 chapters are pretty straight forward and super fun the more you play the harder it gets to figure out exactly what they want you to do, but just use what you already were doing in the chapters before and you should be fine. Chapter 4 is where it starts to get a bit hard as they stop "guiding" you to find clues, you have to manually find them. Takes a bit longer but all in all still pretty much what you were already doing. 

As for the mini games the only one I struggled with was the public influence game, but a little google search and someone has the instructions posted and they are amazing and way better than they guy that tried to explain what to do in game. Was not hard to figure out what to do after reading them so I would recommend using them. 

The story line and major twist that happens in this game is not at all what I was expecting. I read a few reviews so I knew there was going to be something, but wow my brain went no where near where they went. It was a super cool aspect and I can not wait to play the second game.

review_text_raw:
Cyber Manhunt is a comprehensive internet sleuth game from Chinese developers, Aluba Studio. Players must search the darkest online corners to discover pivotal information. Similar to the [i]Orwell[/i] games but with a more sinister story, the title is sure to appease fans of the genre. However, it is not without its flaws and unfortunately suffers from lacklustre text due to its abysmally poor translation.

[b] [u]Pros[/u] [/b]
[list]
    [*] 5 extensive chapters that are all cleverly entwined.
    [*] Differing endings.
    [*] Inventive puzzles & minigames throughout.
    [*] Covers grim themes of crime and corruption.
    [*] Pleasant & simple user interface.
[/list]

[b] [u]Cons[/u] [/b]
[list]
    [*] Awful translation to English, dialogue can come across as robotic and insincere.
    [*] Cumbersome text scenes which do not flow naturally.
    [*] Lacks explanation of puzzle mechanics.
[/list]

[h1]Story: Malignant Data Corruption & Cybersecurity[/h1]
Cyber Manhunt features 5 extensive chapters which range from 1-3 hours each, depending on personal playstyle. Each chapter tackles new persons of interest and a seemingly unrelated story which all comes together upon completion of the game. The stories do feature quite sensitive themes including rape, bullying, female slave imprisonment and more. Whilst there is not any graphic imagery or descriptions, most of the chapters will centre around these topics. Thus, it is important for potential buyers to be aware that it is not an easy-going hacking game and is quite serious in nature.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2544733102

Players begin working for Titan, a large data storage company that can access unlimited personal information about the citizens of Allivia. Our job is to track down specific material to uncover the answers Titan seeks, typically involved in crime investigations or missing persons. The game purposefully questions the indefinite power of having easy access to this data and focuses on the consequences. Moral questions begin to arise, are we helping citizens or doing more damage than good? What is the goal of Titan? Is it something to be proud of?

Soon enough, the corruption can no longer be ignored and a self-proclaimed prophetic persona appears with vengeance for large data companies. Putting Titan in a negative spotlight and allowing players to shape the final acts.

[b] [u]Translation Issues[/u] [/b]
Unfortunately, the biggest disappointment of Cyber Manhunt was its poor translation. Although everything "made sense" and I knew what was going on, the general flow of dialogue was poorly executed. It was easily recognisable that some sections were a direct translation to English and sounded robotic. There were also an abundance of grammar issues and just misspellings such as "CIO" (CEO), "Browbe" (bribe?). Typically, I would not be too bothered as I enjoyed the gameplay immensely, but in a text-based online investigative game, it vastly impacted the games entirety and diminished the serious themes the developers attempt to convey. Some conversations were just laughable and came across as extremely fake. I understand that the Chinese developers are not native English speakers and the Indie nature of the title may prevent proper translation due to funding/time constraints, but it really was abysmal in parts, considering dialogue and text are the sole premise of the title. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2546018709

[h1]Gameplay: Online Investigations, Puzzles & Minigames[/h1]
Majority of the game will be spent on a simple computer interface with access to very familiar applications, "Toothbook", "Gogo" and more. Players must use these programs to uncover information about a specific person. At the beginning of each chapter, we are typically only given the person’s name and a few bits of information. The name can be pasted into "Gogo" to find their "Toothbook" which will unveil their nicknames, hobbies, marital status, friends and so forth, furthering the investigation. This information is all collated into their profiles.

Useful information will be highlighted in red once the cursor scrolls over it, signalling that it can be collected. There are also a handful of other useful applications which can be used as phishing or anonymous calling. Once private information such as DOB is revealed, this can be used in the "Crack" program to obtain passwords. Essentially, keep finding more information which will unlock access to more pertinent data needed to complete the chapter. I found the data-collection to be much more complex than I had originally thought, with lots of different accounts, programs and areas to explore, it was difficult to keep track of it all. But this is in no way a criticism, I enjoyed the more challenging approach and it gave me a sense of achievement when new clues were discovered.

Scour through webpages, emails, private chats and assemble the clues to reveal the full story. There are 4 goals within each chapter and when one goal is fulfilled to 100%, players can enter "reasoning" mode which is essentially a minigame (which differs each time) that puts the story in chronological order and makes sense of all data already obtained.

[b] [u]Minigames & Puzzles[/u] [/b]
Despite this style of game being somewhat monotonous in design and virtually boils down to information-finding, it does include a myriad of minigames to spice things up. Minigames include "hacking" scenes with specific order-based puzzles, matching symbols in a designated layout. Another example was a more strategy-focused section where players must control the popularity of media articles in each state of the country. I found most of these puzzles to be rather inventive and thought-provoking, without succumbing to lazy mechanics or overusing the same concepts, it was kept fresh and interesting.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2548412313

Where this section failed was in its explanation of these puzzles. Sometimes there was a seemingly in-depth cinematic description of what was required, yet it was executed poorly and ultimately caused even more confusion. Other times, no attempt at an explanation was made and I was left with a daunting map filled with things to interact with that I had no idea of their purpose. Even worse, majority of the puzzles are timed and without any indication of what to do (with pausing also disabled), I had to figure it out by trial and error, which was easy enough but of course wastes time and typically resulted in me having to redo the section from scratch.

[h1]Graphics & Sound[/h1]
Being a cyber/hacking simulation title, there is little to comment on in terms of graphics, but the simple interface is clean and very straightforward. There are a handful of cinematic scenes that are actually quite decent and felt reminiscent of comic style art.

Some characters are voiced, as well as calls. The voice-overs are mediocre but do their job. The foreboding soundtrack is on a loop and felt nostalgic of investigative crime TV shows, almost putting pressure on players to uncover clues faster.


[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Cyber Manhunt is an excellent online investigative game, taking inspiration from games such as [i]Orwell[/i] and [i]Papers Please[/i]. Its extensive chapters have an abundance of clues to discover, with countless puzzles and minigames to complete along the way. Despite suffering from severe translation issues which greatly impacted the dialogues flow, the gameplay holds strong and should appeal to any fans of the aforementioned titles. Taking approximately 10-14 hours to complete with differing endings and many achievements encouraging replays, for $15AUD, I highly recommend it to all who love an extensive online lurk.

review_text_raw:
I became intrigued by the game based upon the concept and decided to purchase it while it was still in early access, however, did not fully delve into the game until it was fully released.

[h1] Gameplay loop [/h1]
The basic principle the game follows is that you are working for a company named Titan Matrix, and are assigned cases where you need to investigate a specific person or event. This is done by investigating a person’s online presence, gathering information from for example articles, messaging services and social media. While the game might have the tag of “hacking” this game play element is reduced to using automatic tools for cracking passwords or invading someone’s phone. Most of the game play consists of the player searching for possible clues, in most of the game automatically highlighted in red while moving the cursor over them, with the notable exception starting Chapter 4 where the player can choose the play the chapter without this assisting tool. The found clues can then be used to investigate other events and uncover more of the story. As a last note, not all clues need to be found to solve a case, however finding all can show a new perspective on the story,

[h1] Story [/h1]
As stated earlier, you are working for a company named Titan Matrix. Your job is to uncover the reasons why certain events occurred during the game by investigating the people involved. The reason for this seems to be financial or even political gain for the company. Story lines from earlier chapters do pop up in the later chapters, and do play a part in the events that unfold. [spoiler] This leads to a conflict with a hacker (the main antagonist), who is seemingly doing the same thing as you and seems to know you quite well [/spoiler] For now I will leave it at this, as this is primarily a story-driven game.

[h1] Strengths [/h1]
The game has a nice design and art style with an intuitive user interface making it easy to get into. The story line despite becoming more convoluted as the game progresses manages to capture and hold the player’s attention without overstaying its welcome. The core idea is something many people can relate to, as I can imagine quite a few people fell into the rabbit hole of researching someone online.

[h1] Weaknesses [/h1]
There are a few glaring issues currently in the game. 

[b] Language [/b]
For a story driven game there are quite a few grammatical and/or spelling errors. While this seems to have improved over time this issue still persists. This can easily lead to immersion being broken, or in the worst case confusing clues halting progress. The worst offenders seem to be passwords that are based upon dates, as most of the time the format YYYY-MM-DD is used, but in rare cases a format such as MM-DD-YYYY occurs, leading to unnecessary frustration. Overall, some issues in translation can be overlooked, but the sometimes confusing clues or weird formatting of certain clues are an issue I would implore the developers to address.


[spoiler] [b] Chapter 4: Public Opinion [/b]
At the end of the fourth chapter a certain mini-game needs to be played where the goal is to sway the public opinion. After retrying this section multiple times I just made a spreadsheet noting down all the results from my inputs, and then replayed it with “perfect” inputs, and still had difficulty. This mini-game is not much of a puzzle as it is a test of endurance and trial-and-error. This mini-game is not intuitive in the slightest and unnecessarily difficult. I implore the developers to either change the set-up of this mini-game, or at the least write a better explanation for this mini-game. [/spoiler]

[b] Puzzles and phishing [/b]
While the smallest issue, I did find that the difficulty for certain puzzles are very odd. Some puzzles are incredibly easy, to the point I would hardly argue that they are even puzzles. While others can suddenly be quite difficult. Some of these more difficult puzzles are quite clever in hindsight, but when looking at a broader definition of the word and including the phishing “puzzles” these seem to sometimes lack rhyme or reason, quickly devolving into trail-and-error. Perhaps this latter part is also due to the issues with the translation. As DLC seems to be in the works currently, I would like the developers to reassess how they set-up these phishing sections, as a simple rewrite of dialogue options might not solve the issue.

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]
While this game is far from perfect it is an admirable attempt from a young studio. It is a fun short delve into a concept that is becoming more and more to the forefront in current day society. While I primarily focused on the flaws in this review (in an effort to help the reader know the current issues as well as bring them to the developers attention) I can wholeheartedly say that I did enjoy my time with this game and found it to be worth the couple of euros I put down for it. While the story at times predictable it did enough to lure me in and left me wanting more. I will most likely be back for the sequel/DLC.

[i]As the studio still seems to be pushing updates and fixing some of the issues this review might be updated in the future to more accurately represent the state of the game. [/i]

review_text_raw:
An ok attempt at whatever this genre is, it's no The Operator, but it's (mostly) playable and very rough around the edges, being riddled with terrible ESL dialogue that ChatGPT could've done a better job at generating. This game is translated from Chinese so that accounts for some of those issues, but worse are that some of the "puzzles" are just incomprehensible nonsense based off of bad information the game gives you. In places like the "symbols" password or the phone unlock pattern for Jim's phone you will basically have to use a guide because you aren't given correct information, or an indicator that you have bad information and need to work around it.
